newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Success of National Front stuns French mainstream.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Success of National Front stuns French mainstream.

text.p: Hard-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen is riding high a year from a general election which he predicts will consolidate the role of his National Front party as a major force in French politics.

The Front, which has no seats in parliament now, believes it can have a significant impact on the March 1998 national vote after taking control of its first four town halls in municipal elections in southern France over the past two years.
Front leaders can barely contain their glee over successes of the last year as they prepare for a party congress in Strasbourg at the end of this month.
Moreover, it sometimes seems that France's ruling conservatives are adopting, and perhaps legitimising, Le Pen's agenda of immigration, law and order and economic nationalism.
The Front's three-day congress starting on March 28 will elect a new central committee, appoint a new politburo and re-elect its 68-year-old founder-president.
Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election and refuses to discuss an eventual successor, will be unopposed, Front spokesman Alain Vizier says.

In a reflection of the party's growing strength, 3,000 candidates will vie for the 100 seats on the central committee, Vizier said. The political bureau's 40 members are proposed by the new president, with the central committee's concurrence.
FRONT COULD KNOCK CENTRE-RIGHT FROM POWER
A strong showing by the Front next year could conceivably knock the centre-right out of government and let the left back in, although polls suggest that is unlikely.

By playing on France's record 12.7 percent unemployment, fear of crime and official corruption, Le Pen hopes to become a power broker in run-offs in hundreds of constituencies where mainstream candidates fail to win a clear first-round victory.
The leaders of the mainstream parties have refused to cut deals with the Front in exchange for its support, arguing it would be morally wrong.
Political analysts and pollsters estimate the Front could end up on the second ballot, potentially holding the balance of power, in between 150 and 220 of France's 577 constituencies.
The party has been gaining influence despite tireless efforts by mainstream politicians and action groups to paint it as a racist pariah which should have no place in politics.
"The National Front is driving them crazy," the extreme-right daily Present trumpeted in a recent banner headline.
Artists and intellectuals accuse the party of extremism in its racially tinged rhetoric demanding the expulsion of millions of immigrants and a "French preference" in jobs and welfare.
But they are beginning to realise that the never-ending stream of bad publicity about the Front only seems to strengthen Le Pen's hand.
With all eyes glued on its every action, the Front appears to be setting the national political agenda as other parties look on aghast.
APPEAL STRONG DESPITE NEGATIVE IMAGE
It is not that most French voters are right-wing extremists.
But opinion polls have found that many agree with at least some of Le Pen's ideas and may at times be willing to vote for Front candidates.
"There is a clear gap between the National Front's negative image and the appeal of some of its political positions," said Hugues Cazenave of the IPSOS polling firm.

While mainstream politicians were shocked by Le Pen's presidential score, "let us note that 32 percent of the French people feel quite or somewhat close to the ideas expounded by the National Front on the subject of immigration," he wrote.

Hence the vehemence of last month's debate over government moves to tighten the law against illegal immigration, with the left-wing opposition accusing the centre-right coalition of pandering to the far-right and fostering racism and xenophobia.
Tens of thousands of artists and intellectuals signed petitions condemning the bill and vowing civil disobedience. About 100,000 protesters marched in the streets of Paris.
But when the dust had settled, a series of polls found a solid majority of the public favoured the tighter laws.

Former interior minister Charles Pasqua said the established parties had left Le Pen an open field by abandoning traditional values such as patriotism and nationalism. Le Pen is a virulent opponent of the Maastricht treaty on European union.

"The National Front is not the problem. The problem is the political parties' inability to address the French peoples' concerns," said Pasqua, a senior member of President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR party who once said that Gaullist and National Front voters "share the same values".
"If you want to block extremist movements, you must not allow them exclusive access to the ideas that used to belong to the major parties," he said.

Other analysts say the biggest factor driving the Front's rise is now no longer immigration or law and order, on which voters give the government relatively high marks, but the perception that the established parties are all corrupt.
Despite its steadily growing popularity, the Front often appears to be its own worst enemy.

Le Pen has scandalised the public on more than one occasion with inflammatory rhetoric such as a 1986 remark that Nazi gas chambers were just a "detail of history" or his espousal last year of racial inequality.
Le Pen, who denies he is racist or anti-Semitic, caused outrage again this month when a new book quoted him as having said that Chirac was in the pay of Jewish groups.

The authors said Le Pen told them that Chirac had made a commitment to the B'nai Brith and "other foreign societies" never to form an alliance with the National Front in exchange for huge sums of money. Le Pen denied making the remarks.

Catherine Megret, wife of the party's number two Bruno Megret, said after winning the mayoral election in the southern town of Vitrolles last month that she wanted to end benefits to immigrants, remove left-wing books from the public library and replace social workers with more police.
Megret, who defeated a Socialist incumbent tarred by corruption allegations, also planned to bar state subsidies for concerts by rap musicians, most of whom are black.

Perhaps to divert public attention from such statements, the Front's leaders say the party will focus on social issues during the general election campaign, reaching out to voters who may be unemployed, angered by generous social benefits for foreigners or fed up with mainstream politics.
The party has already begun organising its own trade unions among public transport employees, the police and prison guards.
